newsitem.title: JAPAN: Bomb-scare forces Japan writer to halt signings.
newsitem.headline: Bomb-scare forces Japan writer to halt signings.

text.p: The winner of one of Japan's most prestigious literary prizes on Friday denounced a self-proclaimed rightist for making bomb threats to Tokyo book stores that forced cancellation of her book-signings this week.

Yu Mi-ri, 28, a Korean resident of Japan and winner of the Akutagawa Prize for serious fiction, said the telephoned threats were "a cowardly challenge to freedom of expression" that deprived her of a chance to meet readers.

Yu's book-signing sessions for the prize-winning novel "Family Cinema" at Tokyo-area book stores this week were cancelled after a man claiming to be a member of an obscure rightist group threatened to plant bombs at the stores unless the sessions were called off.
"A Korean named Yu Mi-ri is making remarks which make fools of Japanese," a clerk at one bookstore quoted the man as saying by telephone.

The man's identity and specific complaint were still unclear, said a spokesman for Kodansha Ltd, publisher of the Japanese-language novel, which depicts relations between scattered members of a family who reunite to make a film about the family.
"We're not sure if the caller was really a rightist and he did not say what novel or what passage he was protesting," a Kodansha spokesman said.
The bomb threats were the first of their kind involving an author published by Kodansha, he said.

Japan has hundreds of self-styled right-wing groups, some affiliated with organised-crime groups, which stage protests and occasional violent attacks against people or groups they accuse of being unpatriotic.
Among rightist targets are journalists or authors who write critical accounts of Japanese World War Two atrocities or who are critical of the Imperial family or other national symbols.

The 600,000 Koreans who live in Japan, many of them descendents of wartime forced labourers, often complain of discrimination in education and employment -- themes that often appear in the minority community's literature and films.
On Monday, a member of a right-wing group crashed a van into the front gate of the home of the brother of Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto. No one was hurt.
Daijiro Hashimoto, governor of Kochi Prefecture on southwestern Shikoku island, had earlier questioned whether Japan should keep the song "Kimigayo" (His Majesty's Reign) as Japan's national anthem.
